A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HR-Extreme dataset and HR-Heim baseline. Their complete text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting evaluations in Table 2, per-variable losses in appendix Tables 3-4, and error-map case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds forecasting results at longer lead times and statistical comparisons of normal and extreme weather variables.

M1.justification: The DBSCAN-based dataset construction, cropping and masking procedures, and HR-Heim architecture remain unchanged. The added training descriptions and longer-lead evaluations do not document a revised algorithm or inference procedure.

E1.justification: Table 3 extends the original one-hour forecasting evaluation to lead times 2-4. Geographic coverage, the 17 extreme-weather types, and the underlying HRRR dataset remain unchanged; the newly disclosed training period does not establish added training coverage.

E2.justification: The original comparison retains HR-Heim, Pangu, FuXi, and NWP, and Figure 1 retains KMeans versus DBSCAN. The added lead-time experiment compares HR-Heim with the existing NWP baseline without changing comparator membership in the retained experiments.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce varying forecast lead times and a matched comparison design in Appendix A.1: 50 normal timestamps from the same area, within 15 days of event boundaries and at least 24 hours from the event. Existing test periods and RMSE evaluation remain unchanged. The newly stated training conditions are disclosures rather than demonstrated protocol revisions.

E4.justification: v2 adds two substantive analysis directions: sensitivity to forecast lead time in Table 3 and physical-variable validation across eight normal-versus-extreme cases in Appendix A.1/Figure 5. These expand the supplementary evidence beyond the retained clustering examples and spatial error heatmaps to temporal robustness and whether selected events exhibit unusual physical conditions.

E5.justification: Appendix A.1 newly documents random sampling of 50 comparison timestamps, and Figure 5 displays normal-value distributions as boxplots alongside extreme-event means. This adds descriptive statistical reporting. Model-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, and formal significance tests remain unreported.

E6.justification: Table 2 and all 552 appendix loss values are unchanged. New Table 3 reports HR-Heim/NWP extreme-weather RMSE of 2.29/4.12, 2.86/5.20, and 3.43/6.04 at lead times 2-4, respectively. Figure 5 adds physical-variable findings for selected extreme events; these supplement the existing results rather than revise same-setting performance.

T1.justification: The dataset tensor definitions and architectural descriptions retain the same mathematical content. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs, and the added empirical analyses introduce no substantive formal derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a 3-km dataset covering 17 extreme-weather types, increased forecasting errors on extremes, and HR-Heim's superior one-hour performance. The additional experiments do not revise these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the longer-lead results as supporting HR-Heim's robustness and the new variable comparisons as evidence that HR-Extreme captures physically unusual events with characteristic patterns. Existing limitations concerning report coverage and omitted phenomena remain. The conclusion still states that testing was limited to one hour, creating tension with Table 3.

D1.justification: v2 newly states that the neural models were trained from scratch on January 2019-June 2020 HRRR data with matched settings and comparable capacity, without HR-Extreme fine-tuning or HR-Heim hyperparameter tuning. It also documents an event index and coordinate conversion. Section 3.4 changes data/code availability from currently available to release upon acceptance; actual external availability is not established by the PDFs.

R1.justification: The same 34 cited works and substantive comparisons with earlier forecasting models and datasets are retained. Changes to author-year citations and bibliographic formatting do not alter research positioning.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact. v2 makes localized revisions to data-selection explanations, adds experimental documentation, divides the appendix into A.1 and A.2, and adopts conference headings and author-year citations.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 3 and the eight-panel Figure 5, adopts the ICLR layout, and shortens Figure 4's caption. Figures 1-4 retain identical image content, while the existing appendix tables retain their structure and are renumbered from Tables 3-5 to Tables 4-6.

improvement.justification: The added lead-time evaluation and matched normal/extreme case analysis strengthen empirical support, while the training disclosures make the original comparisons easier to assess. These are useful, limited gains. The unchanged one-hour-only conclusion conflicts with the added evaluation, and the conditional release statement makes access less clear despite the published-paper header.
